Apple___Apple_scab.symptoms:
• Pathological leaf spots, necrotic lesions, or chlorotic yellowing on Apple foliage.
• Irregular brown leaf margins and wilting of affected leaf canopy.
• Stunted shoot development under severe disease pressure.
Apple___Apple_scab.cause:
• Pathogenic fungal/bacterial micro-organism affecting Apple.
• Favored by warm temperatures, high humidity, and prolonged foliage wetness.
• Spreads via wind, water splash, infected soil, or insect vectors.
Apple___Apple_scab.organic_treatment:
• Prune infected foliage and remove severely diseased plant tissue.
• Spray Copper Octanoate or Neem Extract (1%) bio-fungicide.
• Improve soil health with Trichoderma-enriched organic bio-fertilizer.
Apple___Apple_scab.chemical_treatment:
• Apply broad-spectrum protective fungicide Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Alternate with Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L if fungal origin is suspected.
• Consult local agricultural extension for precise local chemical guidelines.
Apple___Apple_scab.prevention:
🌾 Certified Seed Stock & Soil Priming: Sow certified, disease-free seed stock treated with bio-control agents such as *Trichoderma viride* @ 10 g/kg to build initial seedling defense.
🔄 3-Year Non-Host Crop Rotation: Rotate Apple with non-susceptible crop families for 3 consecutive seasons to disrupt pathogen survival cycles in field soil.
💧 Subterranean Drip Irrigation: Irrigate strictly at soil root zones via drip tape lines, completely avoiding overhead leaf watering to maintain foliage dryness.
🌿 Canopy Spacing & Aeration: Space plants adequately during transplanting to promote fast leaf canopy drying after rain events and prevent micro-climate humidity build-up.
🛡️ Field Sanitation & Debris Removal: Clear, compost, or deep-plow all crop residues post-harvest, and maintain weed-free field perimeters to prevent overwintering pathogen persistence.

Apple___Black_rot.symptoms:
• Characteristic V-shaped chlorotic yellow lesions at leaf margins pointing toward stem.
• Darkening of leaf veins turning black, forming a prominent net-like pattern.
• Stems show internal vascular blackening and dwarfed head development.
Apple___Black_rot.cause:
• Bacterial pathogen *Xanthomonas campestris* pv. *campestris*.
• Enters leaves through hydathodes at leaf edges or mechanical wounds.
• Favored by warm moist conditions (24°C–30°C) and heavy rain.
Apple___Black_rot.organic_treatment:
• Prune infected leaves and destroy plant debris by deep burial.
• Spray bio-bactericide *Pseudomonas fluorescens* @ 5 g/L foliar spray.
• Incorporate mustard green manure into soil prior to planting.
Apple___Black_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Soak seeds in Streptomycin Sulfate solution (100 ppm) for 30 mins.
• Apply Copper Hydroxide @ 2.0 g/L mixed with Mancozeb @ 2.0 g/L.
• Repeat spraying at 10-day intervals during wet periods.
Apple___Black_rot.prevention:
🌾 Seed Sanitization & Resistant Hybrids: Use hot-water treated seeds or soak in *Streptomyces* bio-bactericide solution. Choose bacterial spot/rot resistant hybrid cultivars.
🔄 Multi-Year Crop Diversification: Rotate fields with non-susceptible crop families (Maize, Legumes, Alliums) for 3 to 4 years to break bacterial pathogen persistence in soil.
💧 Subsurface Drip & Dew Management: Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation. Refrain from working, weeding, or harvesting in crop fields when foliage is wet from morning dew or recent rain.
🌿 Equipment & Tool Disinfection: Sterilize pruning shears, harvest knives, tractors, and spray rigs between rows using a 70% isopropyl alcohol or quaternary ammonium disinfectant solution.
🛡️ Windbreak Barriers & Weed Clearing: Plant peripheral taller crop windbreaks (Sorghum or Pearl Millet) to intercept wind-driven rain splash, and clear wild host weeds around field perimeters.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.symptoms:
• Numerous raised, powdery orange-red to rust-brown pustules on lower leaf surface.
• Corresponding yellow chlorotic spots appearing on upper leaf canopy.
• Severe infection leads to leaf curling, drying, and early leaf drop.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.cause:
• Fungal rust pathogens (*Puccinia* / *Uromyces* species).
• Spores (urediniospores) carried efficiently over long distances by wind.
• Requires high relative humidity (>90%) and mild temperatures (18°C–25°C).
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.organic_treatment:
• Prune severely rusted leaves and burn away from field area.
• Apply Wettable Sulfur 80% WP @ 3.0 g/L or 0.5% Neem Oil emulsion.
• Spray bio-agent *Verticillium lecanii* @ 5 g/L to parasitise rust spores.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic Triazole fungicide Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternate with Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Hexaconazole @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Apply at onset of initial pustule formation.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.prevention:
🌾 Resistant Cultivars & Site Selection: Plant resistant crop varieties in open, unshaded fields receiving full sunlight (minimum 6–8 hours daily) to inhibit fungal spore germination.
🔄 Balanced Nitrogen Fertilization: Avoid excessive, late-season synthetic nitrogen applications which stimulate lush tender foliage highly susceptible to rust and powdery mildew spores.
💧 Ground-Level Drip Irrigation: Irrigate crops exclusively at soil base using subterranean drip lines during early morning hours to maintain dry leaf surfaces.
🌿 Canopy Aeration & Pruning: Maintain wide row spacing and perform selective pruning of inner sucker shoots to maximize airflow and minimize micro-climate relative humidity within canopy.
🛡️ Proactive Bio-Barrier Sprays: Apply preventive dusting of elemental sulfur or foliar sprays of *Bacillus amyloliquefaciens* at 14-day intervals prior to initial spore emergence.

Apple___healthy.symptoms:
• Vibrant, uniform green pigmentation across all leaf veins and blade surface.
• Turgid leaf margins with zero spots, necrotic lesions, or fungal pustules.
• Normal vigor and physiological leaf architecture.
Apple___healthy.cause:
• Balanced plant nutrition (N-P-K) and optimal soil pH.
• Favorable environmental temperature and moisture conditions.
• Absence of bacterial, fungal, or viral pathogen infection.
Apple___healthy.organic_treatment:
• Apply well-composted organic mulch around crop drip line.
• Spray foliar bio-stimulants or neem oil solution periodically for protection.
Apple___healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical treatment required.
• Continue regular field monitoring and leaf sampling every 7–10 days.
Apple___healthy.prevention:
🌾 Certified Seed & Planting Hygiene: Always plant certified disease-free seed stock sourced from recognized agricultural seed nurseries. Treat seeds prior to planting with bio-control agents such as *Trichoderma viride* @ 10 g/kg and *Pseudomonas fluorescens* @ 10 g/kg to promote robust root development and early seedling vigor.
🔄 Multi-Year Non-Host Crop Rotation: Practice a strict 3-year crop rotation schedule by rotating Apple with non-host crop families (such as legumes, corn, or small grains). This breaks pathogen life cycles, prevents specialized soil-borne spore accumulation, and improves soil structure and organic matter.
💧 Subterranean Root-Zone Irrigation: Irrigate fields exclusively at the plant soil base using underground drip tape lines. Avoid morning, evening, or nighttime overhead sprinkler watering to keep leaf blades dry, which eliminates leaf wetness hours required for airborne fungal spore germination.
🌿 Canopy Spacing & Airflow Management: Maintain recommended inter-row and intra-row plant spacing (60 cm x 45 cm) during field transplantation. Perform periodic selective pruning of lower crowded sucker foliage to facilitate high airflow and maximum sunlight penetration into the lower canopy.
🛡️ Soil Immunity & Proactive Scouting: Apply well-rotted organic compost enriched with neem cake @ 250 kg/acre to build natural rhizosphere immunity. Conduct systematic weekly field scouting across plots to inspect leaf undersides for early symptoms or insect vectors.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.symptoms:
• Small (2–3 mm), dark, water-soaked angular spots on leaves.
• Lesions dry out, forming translucent parchment-like centers.
• Leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, exposing fruit to sunscald.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.cause:
• Bacterial pathogen *Xanthomonas vesicatoria* species complex.
• Transmitted via infected seed, wind-driven rain splashes, and tools.
• Thrives in high humidity and warm temperatures (25°C–30°C).
Peach___Bacterial_spot.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide spray mixed with Organic Neem Extract.
• Remove and destroy infected foliage during dry weather.
• Sterilize pruning shears between plants using 70% isopropyl alcohol.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 3.0 g/L + Streptocycline @ 60 ppm.
• Apply Kasugamycin 3% SL @ 2.0 mL/L at first sign of disease.
• Re-apply after heavy rain events.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.prevention:
🌾 Seed Sanitization & Resistant Hybrids: Use hot-water treated seeds or soak in *Streptomyces* bio-bactericide solution. Choose bacterial spot/rot resistant hybrid cultivars.
🔄 Multi-Year Crop Diversification: Rotate fields with non-susceptible crop families (Maize, Legumes, Alliums) for 3 to 4 years to break bacterial pathogen persistence in soil.
💧 Subsurface Drip & Dew Management: Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation. Refrain from working, weeding, or harvesting in crop fields when foliage is wet from morning dew or recent rain.
🌿 Equipment & Tool Disinfection: Sterilize pruning shears, harvest knives, tractors, and spray rigs between rows using a 70% isopropyl alcohol or quaternary ammonium disinfectant solution.
🛡️ Windbreak Barriers & Weed Clearing: Plant peripheral taller crop windbreaks (Sorghum or Pearl Millet) to intercept wind-driven rain splash, and clear wild host weeds around field perimeters.

Potato___Early_blight.symptoms:
• Dark brown to black lesions featuring concentric target-like rings.
• Yellow chlorotic halos surrounding mature lower leaf spots.
• Premature leaf senescence and defoliation progressing upward.
Potato___Early_blight.cause:
• Fungal pathogen *Alternaria solani* / *Alternaria grandis*.
• Favored by warm temperatures (24°C–29°C) and frequent leaf wetness.
• Survival in infected crop debris and volunteer solanaceous hosts.
Potato___Early_blight.organic_treatment:
• Prune and burn infected lower leaves immediately upon detection.
• Spray Liquid Copper Fungicide or *Bacillus subtilis* bio-control solution.
• Mulch soil surface to prevent fungal spore splash-back during rain.
Potato___Early_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Alternate with Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L for resistance management.
• Spray at 7–10 day intervals during high risk periods.
Potato___Early_blight.prevention:
🌾 Seed Tuber Sanitation & Bio-Priming: Plant certified disease-free potato seed tubers. Dip tubers prior to planting in a bio-fungicide slurry of *Trichoderma harzianum* @ 10 g/kg or *Pseudomonas fluorescens* @ 10 g/kg to protect emerging shoots against tuber-borne *Alternaria solani* spores.
🔄 3-Season Solanaceous Crop Rotation: Implement a mandatory 3-year crop rotation cycle avoiding solanaceous species (Potato, Tomato, Eggplant, Pepper). Rotate with non-solanaceous cover crops like Mustard, Legumes, or Maize to deplete soil fungal spore populations.
💧 Subsurface Drip Irrigation: Utilize ground drip irrigation tape to deliver moisture directly to root zones. Avoid high-pressure overhead sprinklers which splash soil-borne *Alternaria* spores onto lower foliage and extend leaf wetness duration.
🌿 Protective Soil Mulching & Spacing: Apply a 3-inch layer of clean straw mulch over plant beds to create a physical barrier preventing fungal spore rain-splash from soil onto lower leaves. Maintain recommended plant spacing (60 cm x 45 cm) for optimal canopy drying.
🛡️ Stubble Disposal & Weed Sanitation: Shred and deep-plow crop stubble immediately post-harvest to accelerate organic decomposition of fungal survival structures. Eradicate wild nightshade weed reservoirs along field borders throughout the growing season.

Potato___Late_blight.symptoms:
• Irregular, water-soaked dark green to brownish lesions on leaf margins.
• Delicate white cottony mold growth on lower leaf surface under high humidity.
• Rapid leaf collapse, wilting, and characteristic foul odor in fields.
Potato___Late_blight.cause:
• Oomycete pathogen *Phytophthora infestans*.
• Extremely destructive under cool, moist weather (15°C–22°C, RH >90%).
• Airborne sporangia spreading across multi-kilometer distances in wind.
Potato___Late_blight.organic_treatment:
• Remove and destroy entire severely infected plants immediately.
• Apply Copper Octanoate or Bordeaux mixture (1%) as protective spray.
• Apply bio-fungicide containing *Trichoderma viride* to soil base.
Potato___Late_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic fungicide Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold) @ 2.5 g/L.
• Alternate with Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2.0 g/L or Dimethomorph @ 1.0 g/L.
• Repeat spray every 5–7 days while wet cool conditions persist.
Potato___Late_blight.prevention:
🌾 Cultivar Resistance & Seed Selection: Plant late blight resistant potato cultivars (such as Kufri Girdhari, Kufri Himalini, or resistant hybrids). Source certified disease-free seed tubers from official seed certification agencies.
🔄 High Soil Ridging & Tuber Protection: Maintain prominent, well-drained soil ridges (25–30 cm high) around potato stems to create a physical soil filter that prevents surface *Phytophthora infestans* sporangia from washing down to infect subterranean tubers during heavy rains.
💧 Weather-Based Preventive Spraying: Monitor local agricultural meteorological alerts for cool, humid weather spells (temperatures 15°C–22°C, RH >90%). Apply protective copper octanoate or Bordeaux mixture (1%) sprays *prior* to rainfall events.
🌿 Cull Pile & Volunteer Destruction: Locate and completely destroy all cull tuber disposal piles, volunteer potato sprouts, and wild solanaceous weeds within a 500-meter radius of potato fields to eliminate primary airborne inoculum sources.
🛡️ Vine Killing & Harvest Timing: Apply vine desiccant (or kill tops mechanically) 14 days before harvest. Allow tuber skins to mature completely in dry soil prior to digging to prevent live sporangia contact during harvesting.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.symptoms:
• White to grayish talcum powder-like fungal patches on upper leaf blades.
• Patches expand to cover entire leaf surfaces, stems, and shoots.
• Infected leaves curl upward, turn brown, dry out, and drop off.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.cause:
• Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogens (*Erysiphe* / *Podosphaera* species).
• Favored by dry atmospheric conditions combined with high ambient humidity.
• Thrives in shaded, low-airflow environments.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Spray Potassium Bicarbonate (5 g/L) + Horticultural Oil solution.
• Apply Neem Oil 1% spray every 7 days onto leaf surfaces.
• Spray fresh diluted cow milk emulsion (1:9 ratio with water) in sunshine.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Penconazole 10% EC @ 0.5 mL/L.
• Apply Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for systemic dual protection.
• Spray early when first white dusting spots emerge.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.prevention:
🌾 Resistant Cultivars & Site Selection: Plant resistant crop varieties in open, unshaded fields receiving full sunlight (minimum 6–8 hours daily) to inhibit fungal spore germination.
🔄 Balanced Nitrogen Fertilization: Avoid excessive, late-season synthetic nitrogen applications which stimulate lush tender foliage highly susceptible to rust and powdery mildew spores.
💧 Ground-Level Drip Irrigation: Irrigate crops exclusively at soil base using subterranean drip lines during early morning hours to maintain dry leaf surfaces.
🌿 Canopy Aeration & Pruning: Maintain wide row spacing and perform selective pruning of inner sucker shoots to maximize airflow and minimize micro-climate relative humidity within canopy.
🛡️ Proactive Bio-Barrier Sprays: Apply preventive dusting of elemental sulfur or foliar sprays of *Bacillus amyloliquefaciens* at 14-day intervals prior to initial spore emergence.

Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms:
• Dark brown to black lesions featuring concentric target-like rings.
• Yellow chlorotic halos surrounding mature lower leaf spots.
• Premature leaf senescence and defoliation progressing upward.
Tomato___Early_blight.cause:
• Fungal pathogen *Alternaria solani* / *Alternaria grandis*.
• Favored by warm temperatures (24°C–29°C) and frequent leaf wetness.
• Survival in infected crop debris and volunteer solanaceous hosts.
Tomato___Early_blight.organic_treatment:
• Prune and burn infected lower leaves immediately upon detection.
• Spray Liquid Copper Fungicide or *Bacillus subtilis* bio-control solution.
• Mulch soil surface to prevent fungal spore splash-back during rain.
Tomato___Early_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Alternate with Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L for resistance management.
• Spray at 7–10 day intervals during high risk periods.
Tomato___Early_blight.prevention:
🌾 Seed Heat-Treatment & Bio-Protection: Sow certified disease-free seeds treated with hot water (50°C for 25 mins) and bio-fungicides to neutralize seed-borne fungal and bacterial pathogens.
🔄 Field Crop Rotation Protocol: Execute a strict 3-year non-host crop rotation schedule to starve fungal resting spores and reduce pathogen survival in crop debris.
💧 Drip Irrigation & Canopy Drying: Switch completely to root-zone drip irrigation lines. Ensure field beds are aligned with prevailing wind directions to facilitate fast leaf canopy drying after rainfall.
🌿 Plant Spacing & Straw Mulching: Transplant crops at recommended distances (60x45 cm) and lay clean organic straw mulch to suppress soil-splash fungal spore movement onto lower leaves.
🛡️ Post-Harvest Stubble Sanitation: Burn or deep-plow infected plant residues immediately following harvest. Keep field margins clean of volunteer host weeds throughout the winter season.

Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms:
• Irregular, water-soaked dark green to brownish lesions on leaf margins.
• Delicate white cottony mold growth on lower leaf surface under high humidity.
• Rapid leaf collapse, wilting, and characteristic foul odor in fields.
Tomato___Late_blight.cause:
• Oomycete pathogen *Phytophthora infestans*.
• Extremely destructive under cool, moist weather (15°C–22°C, RH >90%).
• Airborne sporangia spreading across multi-kilometer distances in wind.
Tomato___Late_blight.organic_treatment:
• Remove and destroy entire severely infected plants immediately.
• Apply Copper Octanoate or Bordeaux mixture (1%) as protective spray.
• Apply bio-fungicide containing *Trichoderma viride* to soil base.
Tomato___Late_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic fungicide Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold) @ 2.5 g/L.
• Alternate with Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2.0 g/L or Dimethomorph @ 1.0 g/L.
• Repeat spray every 5–7 days while wet cool conditions persist.

• Irregular brown leaf margins and wilting of affected leaf canopy.
• Stunted shoot development under severe disease pressure.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.cause:
• Pathogenic fungal/bacterial micro-organism affecting Tomato.
• Favored by warm temperatures, high humidity, and prolonged foliage wetness.
• Spreads via wind, water splash, infected soil, or insect vectors.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.organic_treatment:
• Prune infected foliage and remove severely diseased plant tissue.
• Spray Copper Octanoate or Neem Extract (1%) bio-fungicide.
• Improve soil health with Trichoderma-enriched organic bio-fertilizer.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.chemical_treatment:
• Apply broad-spectrum protective fungicide Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Alternate with Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L if fungal origin is suspected.
• Consult local agricultural extension for precise local chemical guidelines.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.prevention:
🌾 Certified Seed Stock & Soil Priming: Sow certified, disease-free seed stock treated with bio-control agents such as *Trichoderma viride* @ 10 g/kg to build initial seedling defense.
🔄 3-Year Non-Host Crop Rotation: Rotate Tomato with non-susceptible crop families for 3 consecutive seasons to disrupt pathogen survival cycles in field soil.
💧 Subterranean Drip Irrigation: Irrigate strictly at soil root zones via drip tape lines, completely avoiding overhead leaf watering to maintain foliage dryness.
🌿 Canopy Spacing & Aeration: Space plants adequately during transplanting to promote fast leaf canopy drying after rain events and prevent micro-climate humidity build-up.
🛡️ Field Sanitation & Debris Removal: Clear, compost, or deep-plow all crop residues post-harvest, and maintain weed-free field perimeters to prevent overwintering pathogen persistence.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms:
• Severe upward cupping and wrinkling of young terminal leaves.
• Pronounced yellow chlorosis along leaf margins and interveinal tissue.
• Stunted bush-like plant growth with severe flower drop and zero fruit set.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cause:
• Begomovirus (*Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus* - TYLCV).
• Transmitted exclusively by insect vector Silverleaf Whitefly (*Bemisia tabaci*).
• Rapid vector multiplication during warm dry weather.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow sticky traps (30–40 traps/acre) to monitor/catch whiteflies.
• Spray Insecticidal Soap or 2% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE).
• Apply *Beauveria bassiana* bio-insecticide @ 5 g/L to control whiteflies.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic insecticide Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 mL/L.
• Alternate with Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Spiromesifen @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Target under-surface of foliage where whitefly nymphs congregate.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.prevention:
🌾 Insect Netting & Seedling Protection: Cover seedling nursery beds with 50-mesh UV-stabilized insect-proof netting to prevent early whitefly and aphid vector feeding during sensitive early growth stages.
🔄 Reflective Silver Mulching: Lay reflective silver-on-black plastic mulch across planting beds to disorient incoming flying insect vectors and suppress weed growth.
💧 Perimeter Barrier Crops: Plant 3–4 border rows of tall non-host barrier crops (such as Corn, Sorghum, or Pearl Millet) around fields to act as a physical trap for insect vectors.
🌿 Vector Monitoring & Sticky Traps: Install yellow sticky traps (30–40 traps/acre) across field plots to continuously monitor and catch whitefly and aphid populations.
🛡️ Resistant Hybrids & Weed Eradication: Plant certified virus-resistant hybrids and clear weed reservoir hosts (Solanaceous and Malvaceous weeds) within 100 meters of crop fields.

Tomato___healthy.symptoms:
• Vibrant, uniform green pigmentation across all leaf veins and blade surface.
• Turgid leaf margins with zero spots, necrotic lesions, or fungal pustules.
• Normal vigor and physiological leaf architecture.
Tomato___healthy.cause:
• Balanced plant nutrition (N-P-K) and optimal soil pH.
• Favorable environmental temperature and moisture conditions.
• Absence of bacterial, fungal, or viral pathogen infection.
Tomato___healthy.organic_treatment:
• Apply well-composted organic mulch around crop drip line.
• Spray foliar bio-stimulants or neem oil solution periodically for protection.
Tomato___healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical treatment required.
• Continue regular field monitoring and leaf sampling every 7–10 days.
Tomato___healthy.prevention:
🌾 Certified Seed & Planting Hygiene: Always plant certified disease-free seed stock sourced from recognized agricultural seed nurseries. Treat seeds prior to planting with bio-control agents such as *Trichoderma viride* @ 10 g/kg and *Pseudomonas fluorescens* @ 10 g/kg to promote robust root development and early seedling vigor.
🔄 Multi-Year Non-Host Crop Rotation: Practice a strict 3-year crop rotation schedule by rotating Tomato with non-host crop families (such as legumes, corn, or small grains). This breaks pathogen life cycles, prevents specialized soil-borne spore accumulation, and improves soil structure and organic matter.
💧 Subterranean Root-Zone Irrigation: Irrigate fields exclusively at the plant soil base using underground drip tape lines. Avoid morning, evening, or nighttime overhead sprinkler watering to keep leaf blades dry, which eliminates leaf wetness hours required for airborne fungal spore germination.
🌿 Canopy Spacing & Airflow Management: Maintain recommended inter-row and intra-row plant spacing (60 cm x 45 cm) during field transplantation. Perform periodic selective pruning of lower crowded sucker foliage to facilitate high airflow and maximum sunlight penetration into the lower canopy.
🛡️ Soil Immunity & Proactive Scouting: Apply well-rotted organic compost enriched with neem cake @ 250 kg/acre to build natural rhizosphere immunity. Conduct systematic weekly field scouting across plots to inspect leaf undersides for early symptoms or insect vectors.

apple_alternaria_blotch.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
apple_alternaria_blotch.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
apple_alternaria_blotch.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
apple_alternaria_blotch.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
apple_alternaria_blotch.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

apple_aphis_spp.symptoms:
• Clustering of sap-sucking nymphs/adults or cottony white colonies on leaf undersides, growing tips, and bark.
• Foliar stippling, chlorotic flecking, bronze leaf discoloration, fine webbing, and curling of tender terminal shoots.
• Copious honeydew excretion fostering black sooty mold development over leaves and fruit.
apple_aphis_spp.cause: Foliar insect pest or phytophagous mite infestation. High reproduction rates favored by warm, dry weather and lack of natural beneficial predators.
apple_aphis_spp.organic_treatment:
• Release biological predators: Ladybird beetles (Coccinellids) or Green lacewing larvae (Chrysoperla carnea).
• Apply horticultural mineral oil (1-2%) or Beauveria bassiana entomopathogenic fungus (5 g/L).
• Use strong water jets to dislodge colonies from young shoots.
apple_aphis_spp.chemical_treatment:
• For Mites: Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 mL/L.
• For Aphids/Thrips: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 mL/L or Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L.
• Ensure thorough coverage of the underside of leaves.
apple_aphis_spp.prevention:
• Conserve beneficial insect habitat by planting flowering border strips (coriander, marigold, fennel).
• Avoid indiscriminate use of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that destroy predatory mite populations.
• Inspect nursery seedlings rigorously before transplanting into main fields.

apple_black_rot.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
apple_black_rot.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
apple_black_rot.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
apple_black_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
apple_black_rot.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

apple_brown_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
apple_brown_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
apple_brown_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
apple_brown_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
apple_brown_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

apple_cedar_apple_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
apple_cedar_apple_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
apple_cedar_apple_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
apple_cedar_apple_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
apple_cedar_apple_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

apple_mosaic_virus.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
apple_mosaic_virus.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
apple_mosaic_virus.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
apple_mosaic_virus.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
apple_mosaic_virus.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

apple_powdery_mildew.symptoms:
• Talcum powder-like white to grayish fungal patches coating young leaves, stems, buds, and fruit clusters.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
apple_powdery_mildew.cause: Erysiphales (Ascomycete fungus). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
apple_powdery_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
apple_powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.5 mL/L, Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1 g/L, or Dinocap 48% EC @ 1 mL/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
apple_powdery_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

apple_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
apple_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
apple_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
apple_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
apple_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

Apple___Scab.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
Apple___Scab.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
Apple___Scab.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
Apple___Scab.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.

banana_anthracnose.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
banana_anthracnose.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
banana_anthracnose.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
banana_anthracnose.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
banana_anthracnose.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

banana___bunchy_top.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
banana___bunchy_top.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
banana___bunchy_top.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
banana___bunchy_top.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.

banana_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
banana_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
banana_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
banana_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
banana_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
banana_sigatoka.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
banana_sigatoka.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

basil_downy_mildew.symptoms:
• Angular, yellow-chlorotic patches on upper leaf surface with purplish-grey fungal felt on the underside.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
basil_downy_mildew.cause: Peronosporaceae (Oomycete). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
basil_downy_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
basil_downy_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
basil_downy_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

basil_fusarium_wilt.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
basil_fusarium_wilt.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
basil_fusarium_wilt.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
basil_fusarium_wilt.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
basil_fusarium_wilt.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

basil_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
basil_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
basil_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
basil_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
basil_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

bean_bean_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
bean_bean_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
bean_bean_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
bean_bean_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
bean_bean_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

bean_halo_blight.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
bean_halo_blight.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
bean_halo_blight.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
bean_halo_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
bean_halo_blight.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

bean_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
bean_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
bean_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
bean_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
bean_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

bean_mosaic_virus.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
bean_mosaic_virus.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
bean_mosaic_virus.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
bean_mosaic_virus.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
bean_mosaic_virus.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

blackgram_anthracnose.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
blackgram_anthracnose.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
blackgram_anthracnose.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
blackgram_anthracnose.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
blackgram_anthracnose.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

blackgram_powdery_mildew.symptoms:
• Talcum powder-like white to grayish fungal patches coating young leaves, stems, buds, and fruit clusters.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
blackgram_powdery_mildew.cause: Erysiphales (Ascomycete fungus). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
blackgram_powdery_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
blackgram_powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.5 mL/L, Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1 g/L, or Dinocap 48% EC @ 1 mL/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
blackgram_powdery_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

blackgram_yellow_mosaic.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
blackgram_yellow_mosaic.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
blackgram_yellow_mosaic.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
blackgram_yellow_mosaic.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
blackgram_yellow_mosaic.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

blueberry_anthracnose.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
blueberry_anthracnose.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
blueberry_anthracnose.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
blueberry_anthracnose.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
blueberry_anthracnose.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

blueberry_botrytis_blight.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
blueberry_botrytis_blight.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
blueberry_botrytis_blight.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
blueberry_botrytis_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
blueberry_botrytis_blight.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
blueberry_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
blueberry_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
blueberry_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
blueberry_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

blueberry_scorch.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
blueberry_scorch.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
blueberry_scorch.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
blueberry_scorch.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
blueberry_scorch.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

brassica_black_rot.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
brassica_black_rot.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
brassica_black_rot.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
brassica_black_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
brassica_black_rot.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

broccoli_downy_mildew.symptoms:
• Angular, yellow-chlorotic patches on upper leaf surface with purplish-grey fungal felt on the underside.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
broccoli_downy_mildew.cause: Peronosporaceae (Oomycete). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
broccoli_downy_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
broccoli_downy_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
broccoli_downy_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

cabbage_black_rot.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
cabbage_black_rot.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
cabbage_black_rot.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
cabbage_black_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
cabbage_black_rot.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

cabbage_downy_mildew.symptoms:
• Angular, yellow-chlorotic patches on upper leaf surface with purplish-grey fungal felt on the underside.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
cabbage_downy_mildew.cause: Peronosporaceae (Oomycete). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
cabbage_downy_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
cabbage_downy_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
cabbage_downy_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

cashew_red_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
cashew_red_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
cashew_red_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
cashew_red_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
cashew_red_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

cashew___red_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.

cassava_bacterial_blight.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
cassava_bacterial_blight.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
cassava_bacterial_blight.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
cassava_bacterial_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
cassava_bacterial_blight.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

cassava_brown_leaf_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
cassava_brown_leaf_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
cassava_brown_leaf_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
cassava_brown_leaf_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
cassava_brown_leaf_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

cassava_green_mite.symptoms:
• Clustering of sap-sucking nymphs/adults or cottony white colonies on leaf undersides, growing tips, and bark.
• Foliar stippling, chlorotic flecking, bronze leaf discoloration, fine webbing, and curling of tender terminal shoots.
• Copious honeydew excretion fostering black sooty mold development over leaves and fruit.
cassava_green_mite.cause: Foliar insect pest or phytophagous mite infestation. High reproduction rates favored by warm, dry weather and lack of natural beneficial predators.
cassava_green_mite.organic_treatment:
• Release biological predators: Ladybird beetles (Coccinellids) or Green lacewing larvae (Chrysoperla carnea).
• Apply horticultural mineral oil (1-2%) or Beauveria bassiana entomopathogenic fungus (5 g/L).
• Use strong water jets to dislodge colonies from young shoots.
cassava_green_mite.chemical_treatment:
• For Mites: Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 mL/L.
• For Aphids/Thrips: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 mL/L or Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L.
• Ensure thorough coverage of the underside of leaves.
cassava_green_mite.prevention:
• Conserve beneficial insect habitat by planting flowering border strips (coriander, marigold, fennel).
• Avoid indiscriminate use of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that destroy predatory mite populations.
• Inspect nursery seedlings rigorously before transplanting into main fields.

cassava_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
cassava_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
cassava_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.

cassava_mosaic.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
cassava_mosaic.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
cassava_mosaic.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
cassava_mosaic.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
cassava_mosaic.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

cassava_red_mite.symptoms:
• Clustering of sap-sucking nymphs/adults or cottony white colonies on leaf undersides, growing tips, and bark.
• Foliar stippling, chlorotic flecking, bronze leaf discoloration, fine webbing, and curling of tender terminal shoots.
• Copious honeydew excretion fostering black sooty mold development over leaves and fruit.
cassava_red_mite.cause: Foliar insect pest or phytophagous mite infestation. High reproduction rates favored by warm, dry weather and lack of natural beneficial predators.
cassava_red_mite.organic_treatment:
• Release biological predators: Ladybird beetles (Coccinellids) or Green lacewing larvae (Chrysoperla carnea).
• Apply horticultural mineral oil (1-2%) or Beauveria bassiana entomopathogenic fungus (5 g/L).
• Use strong water jets to dislodge colonies from young shoots.
cassava_red_mite.chemical_treatment:
• For Mites: Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 mL/L.
• For Aphids/Thrips: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 mL/L or Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L.
• Ensure thorough coverage of the underside of leaves.
cassava_red_mite.prevention:
• Conserve beneficial insect habitat by planting flowering border strips (coriander, marigold, fennel).
• Avoid indiscriminate use of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that destroy predatory mite populations.
• Inspect nursery seedlings rigorously before transplanting into main fields.

cassava_root_rot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
cassava_root_rot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
cassava_root_rot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
cassava_root_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
cassava_root_rot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.
