cauliflower_bacterial_soft_rot.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
cauliflower_bacterial_soft_rot.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
cauliflower_bacterial_soft_rot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
cauliflower_bacterial_soft_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
cauliflower_bacterial_soft_rot.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

cauliflower_black_rot.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
cauliflower_black_rot.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
cauliflower_black_rot.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
cauliflower_black_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
cauliflower_black_rot.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

cauliflower_downy_mildew.symptoms:
• Angular, yellow-chlorotic patches on upper leaf surface with purplish-grey fungal felt on the underside.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
cauliflower_downy_mildew.cause: Peronosporaceae (Oomycete). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
cauliflower_downy_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
cauliflower_downy_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
cauliflower_downy_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

cauliflower_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
cauliflower_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
cauliflower_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
cauliflower_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
cauliflower_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

celery_early_blight.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
celery_early_blight.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
celery_early_blight.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
celery_early_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
celery_early_blight.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

cherry_aphis_spp.symptoms:
• Clustering of sap-sucking nymphs/adults or cottony white colonies on leaf undersides, growing tips, and bark.
• Foliar stippling, chlorotic flecking, bronze leaf discoloration, fine webbing, and curling of tender terminal shoots.
• Copious honeydew excretion fostering black sooty mold development over leaves and fruit.
cherry_aphis_spp.cause: Foliar insect pest or phytophagous mite infestation. High reproduction rates favored by warm, dry weather and lack of natural beneficial predators.
cherry_aphis_spp.organic_treatment:
• Release biological predators: Ladybird beetles (Coccinellids) or Green lacewing larvae (Chrysoperla carnea).
• Apply horticultural mineral oil (1-2%) or Beauveria bassiana entomopathogenic fungus (5 g/L).
• Use strong water jets to dislodge colonies from young shoots.
cherry_aphis_spp.chemical_treatment:
• For Mites: Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 mL/L.
• For Aphids/Thrips: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 mL/L or Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L.
• Ensure thorough coverage of the underside of leaves.
cherry_aphis_spp.prevention:
• Conserve beneficial insect habitat by planting flowering border strips (coriander, marigold, fennel).
• Avoid indiscriminate use of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that destroy predatory mite populations.
• Inspect nursery seedlings rigorously before transplanting into main fields.

cherry_powdery_mildew.symptoms:
• Talcum powder-like white to grayish fungal patches coating young leaves, stems, buds, and fruit clusters.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
cherry_powdery_mildew.cause: Erysiphales (Ascomycete fungus). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
cherry_powdery_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
cherry_powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.5 mL/L, Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1 g/L, or Dinocap 48% EC @ 1 mL/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
cherry_powdery_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

cherry_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
cherry_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
cherry_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
cherry_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
cherry_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

chilli_curl.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
chilli_curl.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
chilli_curl.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
chilli_curl.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
chilli_curl.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

citrus_black_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.

citrus_black_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
citrus_black_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.

citrus_canker.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
citrus_canker.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
citrus_canker.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
citrus_canker.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
citrus_canker.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

citrus_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
citrus_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
citrus_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
citrus_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
citrus_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

coffee_black_rot.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
coffee_black_rot.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
coffee_black_rot.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
coffee_black_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
coffee_black_rot.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
Coffee___Black_Rot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
Coffee___Black_Rot.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

coffee_brown_eye_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
coffee_brown_eye_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
coffee_brown_eye_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
coffee_brown_eye_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
coffee_brown_eye_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

coffee_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
coffee_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
coffee_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
coffee_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
coffee_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

coffee_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
coffee_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
coffee_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
coffee_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
coffee_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

coffee_spider_mites.symptoms:
• Clustering of sap-sucking nymphs/adults or cottony white colonies on leaf undersides, growing tips, and bark.
• Foliar stippling, chlorotic flecking, bronze leaf discoloration, fine webbing, and curling of tender terminal shoots.
• Copious honeydew excretion fostering black sooty mold development over leaves and fruit.
coffee_spider_mites.cause: Foliar insect pest or phytophagous mite infestation. High reproduction rates favored by warm, dry weather and lack of natural beneficial predators.
coffee_spider_mites.organic_treatment:
• Release biological predators: Ladybird beetles (Coccinellids) or Green lacewing larvae (Chrysoperla carnea).
• Apply horticultural mineral oil (1-2%) or Beauveria bassiana entomopathogenic fungus (5 g/L).
• Use strong water jets to dislodge colonies from young shoots.
coffee_spider_mites.chemical_treatment:
• For Mites: Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 mL/L.
• For Aphids/Thrips: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 mL/L or Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L.
• Ensure thorough coverage of the underside of leaves.
coffee_spider_mites.prevention:
• Conserve beneficial insect habitat by planting flowering border strips (coriander, marigold, fennel).
• Avoid indiscriminate use of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that destroy predatory mite populations.
• Inspect nursery seedlings rigorously before transplanting into main fields.

Coffee___Spider_Mites.symptoms:
• Clustering of sap-sucking nymphs/adults or cottony white colonies on leaf undersides, growing tips, and bark.
• Foliar stippling, chlorotic flecking, bronze leaf discoloration, fine webbing, and curling of tender terminal shoots.
• Copious honeydew excretion fostering black sooty mold development over leaves and fruit.

coriander_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
coriander_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
coriander_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
coriander_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
coriander_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

corn_brown_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
corn_brown_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
corn_brown_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
corn_brown_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
corn_brown_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

corn_common_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
corn_common_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
corn_common_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
corn_common_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
corn_common_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

corn_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
corn_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
corn_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
corn_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
corn_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

corn_mildew.symptoms:
• Talcum powder-like white to grayish fungal patches coating young leaves, stems, buds, and fruit clusters.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
corn_mildew.cause: Erysiphales (Ascomycete fungus). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
corn_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
corn_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.5 mL/L, Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1 g/L, or Dinocap 48% EC @ 1 mL/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
corn_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

corn_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
corn_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
corn_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
corn_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
corn_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

corn_smut.symptoms:
• Sori filled with dark black, sooty chlamydospores rupturing floral parts, grain kernels, or whip-like shoots.
• Severe lodging, blank panicles (chaffy grain), and rapid plant collapse.
corn_smut.cause: Fungal pathogen (Magnaporthe oryzae for blast, Colletotrichum falcatum for red rot, Ustilago/Sporisorium for smut). Seed-borne and soil-borne survival with wind/water dispersal.
corn_smut.organic_treatment:
• Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/kg seed before sowing.
• Soil application of Trichoderma viride enriched farmyard manure (2.5 kg/ha).
• Rogue out and incinerate infected whips/plants immediately to prevent spore dispersal.
corn_smut.chemical_treatment:
• For Blast: Tricyclazole 75% WP @ 0.6 g/L or Isoprothiolane 40% EC @ 1.5 mL/L.
• For Red Rot / Smuts: Set/seed dip in Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Carboxin 37.5% + Thiram 37.5% DS @ 2 g/kg seed.
• Apply foliar systemic fungicides at early tillering and panicle emergence.
corn_smut.prevention:
• Use certified disease-free certified seed stock or hot-water treated sets (52°C for 30 mins).
• Avoid excessive nitrogenous fertilizers; split nitrogen applications with potassium.
• Implement field drainage to avoid prolonged stagnation in low-lying patches.

corn_streak_virus.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
corn_streak_virus.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
corn_streak_virus.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
corn_streak_virus.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
corn_streak_virus.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
corn_violet_decoloration.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

Corn___Violet_Decoloration.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
Corn___Violet_Decoloration.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
Corn___Violet_Decoloration.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.

cotton_bacterial_blight.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
cotton_bacterial_blight.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
cotton_bacterial_blight.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
cotton_bacterial_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
cotton_bacterial_blight.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

cotton_curl_virus.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
cotton_curl_virus.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
cotton_curl_virus.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
cotton_curl_virus.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
cotton_curl_virus.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

cotton_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
cotton_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
cotton_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
cotton_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
cotton_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

cotton___healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.

cotton_powdery_mildew.symptoms:
• Talcum powder-like white to grayish fungal patches coating young leaves, stems, buds, and fruit clusters.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
cotton_powdery_mildew.cause: Erysiphales (Ascomycete fungus). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
cotton_powdery_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
cotton_powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.5 mL/L, Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1 g/L, or Dinocap 48% EC @ 1 mL/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
cotton_powdery_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

cotton_target_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
cotton_target_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
cotton_target_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
cotton_target_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
cotton_target_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

cucumber_anthracnose.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
cucumber_anthracnose.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
cucumber_anthracnose.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
cucumber_anthracnose.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
cucumber_anthracnose.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

cucumber_bacterial_wilt.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
cucumber_bacterial_wilt.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
cucumber_bacterial_wilt.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
cucumber_bacterial_wilt.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
cucumber_bacterial_wilt.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
cucumber_gummy_stem_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
cucumber_gummy_stem_blight.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

cucumber_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
cucumber_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
cucumber_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
cucumber_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
cucumber_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

cucumber_powdery_mildew.symptoms:
• Talcum powder-like white to grayish fungal patches coating young leaves, stems, buds, and fruit clusters.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
cucumber_powdery_mildew.cause: Erysiphales (Ascomycete fungus). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
cucumber_powdery_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
cucumber_powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.5 mL/L, Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1 g/L, or Dinocap 48% EC @ 1 mL/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
cucumber_powdery_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

eggplant_phomopsis_fruit_rot.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
eggplant_phomopsis_fruit_rot.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
eggplant_phomopsis_fruit_rot.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
eggplant_phomopsis_fruit_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
eggplant_phomopsis_fruit_rot.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

garlic_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
garlic_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
garlic_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
garlic_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
garlic_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

grape_black_rot.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
grape_black_rot.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
grape_black_rot.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
grape_black_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
grape_black_rot.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

grape_downy_mildew.symptoms:
• Angular, yellow-chlorotic patches on upper leaf surface with purplish-grey fungal felt on the underside.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
grape_downy_mildew.cause: Peronosporaceae (Oomycete). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
grape_downy_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
grape_downy_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
grape_downy_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

grape_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
grape_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
grape_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
grape_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.

grape_leaf_blight.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
grape_leaf_blight.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
grape_leaf_blight.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
grape_leaf_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
grape_leaf_blight.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

guava_canker.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
guava_canker.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
guava_canker.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
guava_canker.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
guava_canker.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

guava_red_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
guava_red_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
guava_red_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
guava_red_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
guava_red_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

lettuce_downy_mildew.symptoms:
• Angular, yellow-chlorotic patches on upper leaf surface with purplish-grey fungal felt on the underside.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
lettuce_downy_mildew.cause: Peronosporaceae (Oomycete). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
lettuce_downy_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
lettuce_downy_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
lettuce_downy_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

Lettuce___Downy_Mildew_(Peronosporaceae_.symptoms:
• Angular, yellow-chlorotic patches on upper leaf surface with purplish-grey fungal felt on the underside.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
Lettuce___Downy_Mildew_(Peronosporaceae_.cause: Peronosporaceae (Oomycete). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
Lettuce___Downy_Mildew_(Peronosporaceae_.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
Lettuce___Downy_Mildew_(Peronosporaceae_.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
Lettuce___Downy_Mildew_(Peronosporaceae_.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

lettuce_mosaic_virus.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
lettuce_mosaic_virus.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
lettuce_mosaic_virus.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
lettuce_mosaic_virus.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
lettuce_mosaic_virus.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

mango_anthracnose.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
mango_anthracnose.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
mango_anthracnose.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
mango_anthracnose.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
mango_anthracnose.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

mango_apoderus_javanicus.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
mango_apoderus_javanicus.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
mango_apoderus_javanicus.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
mango_apoderus_javanicus.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
mango_apoderus_javanicus.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

mango_bacterial_canker.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
mango_bacterial_canker.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
mango_bacterial_canker.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
mango_bacterial_canker.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
mango_bacterial_canker.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

mango_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
mango_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
mango_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
mango_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
mango_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

mango_powdery_mildew.symptoms:
• Talcum powder-like white to grayish fungal patches coating young leaves, stems, buds, and fruit clusters.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
mango_powdery_mildew.cause: Erysiphales (Ascomycete fungus). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
mango_powdery_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
mango_powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.5 mL/L, Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1 g/L, or Dinocap 48% EC @ 1 mL/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
mango_powdery_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
maple___tar_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
maple___tar_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

olive_aculus_olearius.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.

olive_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
olive_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
olive_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
olive_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
olive_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

paddy_bacterial_blight.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
paddy_bacterial_blight.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
paddy_bacterial_blight.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
paddy_bacterial_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
paddy_bacterial_blight.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

paddy_black_stem_borer.symptoms:
• Clustering of sap-sucking nymphs/adults or cottony white colonies on leaf undersides, growing tips, and bark.

paddy_blast.symptoms:
• Spindle-shaped (eye-shaped) lesions with greyish-white centers and reddish-brown borders on leaves, neck, and panicles.
• Severe lodging, blank panicles (chaffy grain), and rapid plant collapse.
paddy_blast.cause: Fungal pathogen (Magnaporthe oryzae for blast, Colletotrichum falcatum for red rot, Ustilago/Sporisorium for smut). Seed-borne and soil-borne survival with wind/water dispersal.
paddy_blast.organic_treatment:
• Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/kg seed before sowing.
• Soil application of Trichoderma viride enriched farmyard manure (2.5 kg/ha).
• Rogue out and incinerate infected whips/plants immediately to prevent spore dispersal.
paddy_blast.chemical_treatment:
• For Blast: Tricyclazole 75% WP @ 0.6 g/L or Isoprothiolane 40% EC @ 1.5 mL/L.
• For Red Rot / Smuts: Set/seed dip in Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Carboxin 37.5% + Thiram 37.5% DS @ 2 g/kg seed.
• Apply foliar systemic fungicides at early tillering and panicle emergence.
paddy_blast.prevention:
• Use certified disease-free certified seed stock or hot-water treated sets (52°C for 30 mins).
• Avoid excessive nitrogenous fertilizers; split nitrogen applications with potassium.
• Implement field drainage to avoid prolonged stagnation in low-lying patches.

paddy_brown_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
paddy_brown_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
paddy_brown_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
paddy_brown_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
paddy_brown_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

paddy_downy_mildew.symptoms:
• Angular, yellow-chlorotic patches on upper leaf surface with purplish-grey fungal felt on the underside.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
paddy_downy_mildew.cause: Peronosporaceae (Oomycete). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
paddy_downy_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
paddy_downy_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
paddy_downy_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.
