paddy_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
paddy_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
paddy_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
paddy_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
paddy_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
paddy___leaf_blight.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
paddy___leaf_blight.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
paddy___leaf_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
paddy___leaf_blight.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

paddy_leafblast.symptoms:
• Spindle-shaped (eye-shaped) lesions with greyish-white centers and reddish-brown borders on leaves, neck, and panicles.
• Severe lodging, blank panicles (chaffy grain), and rapid plant collapse.
paddy_leafblast.cause: Fungal pathogen (Magnaporthe oryzae for blast, Colletotrichum falcatum for red rot, Ustilago/Sporisorium for smut). Seed-borne and soil-borne survival with wind/water dispersal.
paddy_leafblast.organic_treatment:
• Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/kg seed before sowing.
• Soil application of Trichoderma viride enriched farmyard manure (2.5 kg/ha).
• Rogue out and incinerate infected whips/plants immediately to prevent spore dispersal.
paddy_leafblast.chemical_treatment:
• For Blast: Tricyclazole 75% WP @ 0.6 g/L or Isoprothiolane 40% EC @ 1.5 mL/L.
• For Red Rot / Smuts: Set/seed dip in Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Carboxin 37.5% + Thiram 37.5% DS @ 2 g/kg seed.
• Apply foliar systemic fungicides at early tillering and panicle emergence.
paddy_leafblast.prevention:
• Use certified disease-free certified seed stock or hot-water treated sets (52°C for 30 mins).
• Avoid excessive nitrogenous fertilizers; split nitrogen applications with potassium.
• Implement field drainage to avoid prolonged stagnation in low-lying patches.

paddy_tungro.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
paddy_tungro.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
paddy_tungro.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
paddy_tungro.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
paddy_tungro.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

paddy_white_stem_borer.symptoms:
• Clustering of sap-sucking nymphs/adults or cottony white colonies on leaf undersides, growing tips, and bark.
• Foliar stippling, chlorotic flecking, bronze leaf discoloration, fine webbing, and curling of tender terminal shoots.
• Copious honeydew excretion fostering black sooty mold development over leaves and fruit.
paddy_white_stem_borer.cause: Foliar insect pest or phytophagous mite infestation. High reproduction rates favored by warm, dry weather and lack of natural beneficial predators.
paddy_white_stem_borer.organic_treatment:
• Release biological predators: Ladybird beetles (Coccinellids) or Green lacewing larvae (Chrysoperla carnea).
• Apply horticultural mineral oil (1-2%) or Beauveria bassiana entomopathogenic fungus (5 g/L).
• Use strong water jets to dislodge colonies from young shoots.
paddy_white_stem_borer.chemical_treatment:
• For Mites: Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 mL/L.
• For Aphids/Thrips: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 mL/L or Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L.
• Ensure thorough coverage of the underside of leaves.
paddy_white_stem_borer.prevention:
• Conserve beneficial insect habitat by planting flowering border strips (coriander, marigold, fennel).
• Avoid indiscriminate use of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that destroy predatory mite populations.
• Inspect nursery seedlings rigorously before transplanting into main fields.

• Avoid indiscriminate use of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that destroy predatory mite populations.
• Inspect nursery seedlings rigorously before transplanting into main fields.

paddy_yellow_stem_borer.symptoms:
• Clustering of sap-sucking nymphs/adults or cottony white colonies on leaf undersides, growing tips, and bark.
• Foliar stippling, chlorotic flecking, bronze leaf discoloration, fine webbing, and curling of tender terminal shoots.
• Copious honeydew excretion fostering black sooty mold development over leaves and fruit.
paddy_yellow_stem_borer.cause: Foliar insect pest or phytophagous mite infestation. High reproduction rates favored by warm, dry weather and lack of natural beneficial predators.
paddy_yellow_stem_borer.organic_treatment:
• Release biological predators: Ladybird beetles (Coccinellids) or Green lacewing larvae (Chrysoperla carnea).
• Apply horticultural mineral oil (1-2%) or Beauveria bassiana entomopathogenic fungus (5 g/L).
• Use strong water jets to dislodge colonies from young shoots.
paddy_yellow_stem_borer.chemical_treatment:
• For Mites: Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 mL/L.
• For Aphids/Thrips: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 mL/L or Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L.
• Ensure thorough coverage of the underside of leaves.

• Avoid indiscriminate use of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that destroy predatory mite populations.

palm_brown_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
palm_brown_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
palm_brown_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
palm_brown_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
palm_brown_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

palm_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
palm_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
palm_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
palm_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
palm_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

papaya_anthracnose.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
papaya_anthracnose.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
papaya_anthracnose.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
papaya_anthracnose.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
papaya_anthracnose.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

papaya_bacterial_spot.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
papaya_bacterial_spot.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
papaya_bacterial_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
papaya_bacterial_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
papaya_bacterial_spot.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

papaya_curl.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
papaya_curl.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
papaya_curl.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
papaya_curl.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
papaya_curl.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

papaya_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
papaya_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
papaya_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
papaya_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
papaya_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

papaya_ring_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
papaya_ring_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
papaya_ring_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
papaya_ring_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
papaya_ring_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

peach_anthracnose.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
peach_anthracnose.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
peach_anthracnose.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
peach_anthracnose.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
peach_anthracnose.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

peach_bacterial_spot.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
peach_bacterial_spot.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
peach_bacterial_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
peach_bacterial_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
peach_bacterial_spot.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
peach___curl.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

peach_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
peach_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
peach_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
peach_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
peach_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

peach_monillia_laxa.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
peach_monillia_laxa.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
peach_monillia_laxa.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
peach_monillia_laxa.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
peach_monillia_laxa.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

peach_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
peach_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
peach_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
peach_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
peach_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

peanut_late_leaf_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
peanut_late_leaf_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
peanut_late_leaf_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
peanut_late_leaf_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
peanut_late_leaf_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

peanut_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
peanut_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
peanut_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
peanut_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
peanut_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

pear_curl.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
pear_curl.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
pear_curl.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
pear_curl.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
pear_curl.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

pepper_bell_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
pepper_bell_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
pepper_bell_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
pepper_bell_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
pepper_bell_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

pepper_bell_powdery_mildew.symptoms:
• Talcum powder-like white to grayish fungal patches coating young leaves, stems, buds, and fruit clusters.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
pepper_bell_powdery_mildew.cause: Erysiphales (Ascomycete fungus). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
pepper_bell_powdery_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
pepper_bell_powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.5 mL/L, Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1 g/L, or Dinocap 48% EC @ 1 mL/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
pepper_bell_powdery_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

• Talcum powder-like white to grayish fungal patches coating young leaves, stems, buds, and fruit clusters.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
pepper_bell___powdery_mildew.cause: Erysiphales (Ascomycete fungus). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
pepper_bell___powdery_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).

• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.

plum_aphis_spp.symptoms:
• Clustering of sap-sucking nymphs/adults or cottony white colonies on leaf undersides, growing tips, and bark.
• Foliar stippling, chlorotic flecking, bronze leaf discoloration, fine webbing, and curling of tender terminal shoots.
• Copious honeydew excretion fostering black sooty mold development over leaves and fruit.
plum_aphis_spp.cause: Foliar insect pest or phytophagous mite infestation. High reproduction rates favored by warm, dry weather and lack of natural beneficial predators.
plum_aphis_spp.organic_treatment:
• Release biological predators: Ladybird beetles (Coccinellids) or Green lacewing larvae (Chrysoperla carnea).
• Apply horticultural mineral oil (1-2%) or Beauveria bassiana entomopathogenic fungus (5 g/L).
• Use strong water jets to dislodge colonies from young shoots.
plum_aphis_spp.chemical_treatment:
• For Mites: Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 mL/L.
• For Aphids/Thrips: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 mL/L or Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L.
• Ensure thorough coverage of the underside of leaves.
plum_aphis_spp.prevention:
• Conserve beneficial insect habitat by planting flowering border strips (coriander, marigold, fennel).
• Avoid indiscriminate use of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that destroy predatory mite populations.
• Inspect nursery seedlings rigorously before transplanting into main fields.

plum_bacterial_spot.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
plum_bacterial_spot.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
plum_bacterial_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
plum_bacterial_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
plum_bacterial_spot.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

plum_brown_rot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
plum_brown_rot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
plum_brown_rot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
plum_brown_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
plum_brown_rot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

plum_pox_virus.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
plum_pox_virus.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
plum_pox_virus.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
plum_pox_virus.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
plum_pox_virus.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

plum_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
plum_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
plum_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
plum_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
plum_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
plum___rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
plum___rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

potato_early_blight.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
potato_early_blight.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
potato_early_blight.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
potato_early_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
potato_early_blight.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

potato_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
potato_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
potato_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
potato_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
potato_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

pumpkin_powdery_mildew.symptoms:
• Talcum powder-like white to grayish fungal patches coating young leaves, stems, buds, and fruit clusters.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
pumpkin_powdery_mildew.cause: Erysiphales (Ascomycete fungus). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
pumpkin_powdery_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
pumpkin_powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.5 mL/L, Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1 g/L, or Dinocap 48% EC @ 1 mL/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
pumpkin_powdery_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

raspberry_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
raspberry_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
raspberry_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
raspberry_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
raspberry_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

raspberry_yellow_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
raspberry_yellow_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
raspberry_yellow_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
raspberry_yellow_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
raspberry_yellow_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

rose_downy_mildew.symptoms:
• Angular, yellow-chlorotic patches on upper leaf surface with purplish-grey fungal felt on the underside.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
rose_downy_mildew.cause: Peronosporaceae (Oomycete). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
rose_downy_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
rose_downy_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
rose_downy_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

soybean_bacterial_blight.symptoms:
• Water-soaked, angular translucent spots restricted by leaf veins, progressing to brown-black necrotic blights.
• Droplets of milky-yellow bacterial ooze exuding from lesions during humid morning hours.
• Marginal chlorosis ('V'-shaped chlorotic wedges), vascular clogging, rapid daytime wilting, and stem cankers.
soybean_bacterial_blight.cause: Phytopathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas / Pseudomonas / Ralstonia / Candidatus Liberibacter). Enters through natural stomata, hydathodes, and mechanical wounds; spreads via rain-splash and pruning tools.
soybean_bacterial_blight.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L.
• Apply bio-control agent Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) as a prophylactic canopy spray.
• Sanitize all farm equipment and harvesting crates with quaternary ammonium or 10% bleach.
soybean_bacterial_blight.chemical_treatment:
• Combine Copper Oxychloride (2.5 g/L) with Streptomycin Sulphate + Tetracycline (Streptocycline) @ 100-150 ppm (1 g in 10 L water).
• For vascular wilts, drench root zone with Copper Oxychloride (3 g/L).
• Repeat application at 10-12 day intervals if stormy, wet weather persists.
soybean_bacterial_blight.prevention:
• Sow certified disease-free, acid-delinted seeds or tissue-cultured clones.
• Strictly avoid working in or cultivating wet fields to prevent spreading bacterial slime.
• Control insect vectors (psyllids, leafhoppers, beetles) that transmit vascular bacteria.

soybean_caterpillar.symptoms:
• Clustering of sap-sucking nymphs/adults or cottony white colonies on leaf undersides, growing tips, and bark.
• Foliar stippling, chlorotic flecking, bronze leaf discoloration, fine webbing, and curling of tender terminal shoots.
• Copious honeydew excretion fostering black sooty mold development over leaves and fruit.
soybean_caterpillar.cause: Foliar insect pest or phytophagous mite infestation. High reproduction rates favored by warm, dry weather and lack of natural beneficial predators.
soybean_caterpillar.organic_treatment:
• Release biological predators: Ladybird beetles (Coccinellids) or Green lacewing larvae (Chrysoperla carnea).
• Apply horticultural mineral oil (1-2%) or Beauveria bassiana entomopathogenic fungus (5 g/L).
• Use strong water jets to dislodge colonies from young shoots.
soybean_caterpillar.chemical_treatment:
• For Mites: Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 mL/L.
• For Aphids/Thrips: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 mL/L or Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L.
• Ensure thorough coverage of the underside of leaves.
soybean_caterpillar.prevention:
• Conserve beneficial insect habitat by planting flowering border strips (coriander, marigold, fennel).
• Avoid indiscriminate use of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that destroy predatory mite populations.
• Inspect nursery seedlings rigorously before transplanting into main fields.

soybean_downy_mildew.symptoms:
• Angular, yellow-chlorotic patches on upper leaf surface with purplish-grey fungal felt on the underside.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
soybean_downy_mildew.cause: Peronosporaceae (Oomycete). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
soybean_downy_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
soybean_downy_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
soybean_downy_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

soybean_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
soybean_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
soybean_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
soybean_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
soybean_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

soybean_mosaic.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
soybean_mosaic.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
soybean_mosaic.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
soybean_mosaic.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
soybean_mosaic.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
soybean___mosaic.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
soybean___mosaic.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
soybean___mosaic.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
soybean___mosaic.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

soybean_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
soybean_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
soybean_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
soybean_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
soybean_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

squash_powdery_mildew.symptoms:
• Talcum powder-like white to grayish fungal patches coating young leaves, stems, buds, and fruit clusters.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
squash_powdery_mildew.cause: Erysiphales (Ascomycete fungus). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
squash_powdery_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
squash_powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.5 mL/L, Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1 g/L, or Dinocap 48% EC @ 1 mL/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
squash_powdery_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

strawberry_anthracnose.symptoms:
• Sunken, circular to oval water-soaked necrotic lesions with dark concentric rings on foliage, twigs, and fruit.
• Under moist conditions, pinkish to salmon-colored gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) ooze from lesion centers.
• Severe twig dieback (blight), blossom drop, and rapid post-harvest fruit decay.
strawberry_anthracnose.cause: Colletotrichum / Elsinoe fungal species. Spores overwinter in infected plant debris, mummified fruit, and cankers, spreading via rain-splash and overhead irrigation.
strawberry_anthracnose.organic_treatment:
• Apply Copper Hydroxide / Bordeaux mixture (1%) as a thorough canopy wash.
• Spray botanical extracts (Garlic clove extract 5% or Neem seed kernel extract 5%).
• Prune out and burn all dead twigs, mummified fruits, and infected cankers 5 cm below visible infection.
strawberry_anthracnose.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L.
• Alternatively apply Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L.
• Apply at bloom, petal fall, and fruit set stages.
strawberry_anthracnose.prevention:
• Practice strict post-harvest orchard/field sanitation.
• Treat propagation seeds/cuttings with bio-priming agents before planting.
• Provide balanced calcium and potassium nutrition to thicken epidermal cell walls.

strawberry_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
strawberry_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
strawberry_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
strawberry_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
strawberry_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

strawberry_scorch.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
strawberry_scorch.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
strawberry_scorch.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
strawberry_scorch.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
strawberry_scorch.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
Sugarcane___Brown_/_Leaf_Rust_(Puccinia_.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.

sugarcane_brown_spot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
sugarcane_brown_spot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
sugarcane_brown_spot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
sugarcane_brown_spot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
sugarcane_brown_spot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

sugarcane_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
sugarcane_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
sugarcane_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
sugarcane_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
sugarcane_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.

sugarcane_mosaic.symptoms:
• Mottling, interveinal chlorosis, mosaic light/dark green patches, and severe leaf puckering.
• Downward or upward cupping of leaves, thick leathery texture, shortened internodes, and severe plant stunting (witch's broom).
• Flower abortion, malformed fruit with chlorotic rings, and catastrophic yield reduction.
sugarcane_mosaic.cause: Plant viral complex (Begomovirus / Potyvirus / Tobamovirus). Transmitted rapidly by piercing-sucking insect vectors (Bemisia tabaci whiteflies, aphids, thrips) and mechanically via contaminated pruning tools.
sugarcane_mosaic.organic_treatment:
• Install yellow and blue sticky traps (25-30 traps/acre) across the canopy to monitor and trap whiteflies/aphids.
• Spray Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3 mL/L or Fish oil rosin soap (20 g/L) to deter vector feeding.
• Immediately rogue out and bury/burn virus-infected plants to eliminate the vector inoculum reservoir.
sugarcane_mosaic.chemical_treatment:
• Viruses cannot be cured with chemical sprays; target insect vectors with systemic insecticides:
• Spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 0.5 g/L.
• Alternatively spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 mL/L for nymph control.
sugarcane_mosaic.prevention:
• Use virus-tolerant certified hybrid varieties.
• Grow barrier crops (2-3 dense border rows of maize, sorghum, or pearl millet) to intercept incoming wind-borne vectors.
• Use reflective silver plastic mulch to repel flying insect vectors from young transplants.

sugarcane_red_rot.symptoms:
• Internal reddening of pith tissues with transverse white bands, sour alcoholic odor, and premature leaf yellowing/drying.
• Severe lodging, blank panicles (chaffy grain), and rapid plant collapse.
sugarcane_red_rot.cause: Fungal pathogen (Magnaporthe oryzae for blast, Colletotrichum falcatum for red rot, Ustilago/Sporisorium for smut). Seed-borne and soil-borne survival with wind/water dispersal.
sugarcane_red_rot.organic_treatment:
• Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/kg seed before sowing.
• Soil application of Trichoderma viride enriched farmyard manure (2.5 kg/ha).
• Rogue out and incinerate infected whips/plants immediately to prevent spore dispersal.
sugarcane_red_rot.chemical_treatment:
• For Blast: Tricyclazole 75% WP @ 0.6 g/L or Isoprothiolane 40% EC @ 1.5 mL/L.
• For Red Rot / Smuts: Set/seed dip in Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Carboxin 37.5% + Thiram 37.5% DS @ 2 g/kg seed.
• Apply foliar systemic fungicides at early tillering and panicle emergence.
sugarcane_red_rot.prevention:
• Use certified disease-free certified seed stock or hot-water treated sets (52°C for 30 mins).
• Avoid excessive nitrogenous fertilizers; split nitrogen applications with potassium.
• Implement field drainage to avoid prolonged stagnation in low-lying patches.

sugarcane_rust.symptoms:
• Elevated, powdery pustules (uredinia) erupting on upper and lower leaf surfaces, leaf sheaths, and stems.
• Pustule coloration ranges from vibrant orange, reddish-brown to dark brown, releasing millions of powdery spores when touched.
• Severe infection leads to extensive chlorotic halos, premature foliar desiccation, lodging, and significant yield loss.
sugarcane_rust.cause: Obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen (Puccinia / Uromyces spp.). Airborne urediniospores spread rapidly during cool, humid nights (15-22°C) with morning dew periods exceeding 6-8 hours.
sugarcane_rust.organic_treatment:
• Spray wettable sulfur @ 2.5 g/L or potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) at the earliest sign of pustules.
• Apply bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum (5 g/L) to colonize leaf surface.
• Rogue out and burn heavily infected volunteer plants and alternate weed hosts around field margins.
sugarcane_rust.chemical_treatment:
• Apply systemic triazole fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 mL/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Alternatively spray Strobilurin + Triazole combos: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Repeat spray after 12-14 days if cool, damp weather persists.
sugarcane_rust.prevention:
• Plant certified rust-resistant, recommended regional cultivars.
• Avoid excessive top-dressing of nitrogenous fertilizers, which produces lush, highly susceptible foliage.
• Ensure adequate row spacing to facilitate air circulation and rapid canopy drying.

sugarcane_sett_rot.symptoms:
• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
sugarcane_sett_rot.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
sugarcane_sett_rot.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
sugarcane_sett_rot.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
sugarcane_sett_rot.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

sunflower_downy_mildew.symptoms:
• Angular, yellow-chlorotic patches on upper leaf surface with purplish-grey fungal felt on the underside.
• Infected leaves curl upwards, turn brittle, senesce prematurely, and drop.
• Drastic reduction in photosynthetic capacity, blossom drop, and stunted fruit development.
sunflower_downy_mildew.cause: Peronosporaceae (Oomycete). Spreads rapidly under conditions of moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, dense shade, and poor canopy ventilation.
sunflower_downy_mildew.organic_treatment:
• Foliar spray of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate 5 g/L) mixed with horticultural oil (5 mL/L).
• Apply sulfur-based organic dust or Neem oil (0.5% EC) @ 3-5 mL/L at 7-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected shaded canopy leaves to improve interior light penetration.
sunflower_downy_mildew.chemical_treatment:
• Apply Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb @ 2 g/L.
• Apply protective spray during early morning before midday heat.
sunflower_downy_mildew.prevention:
• Maintain wide row spacing and trellis training to maximize sunlight penetration.
• Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that prolongs foliar leaf wetness.
• Clean and disinfect pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between rows.

• Circular to irregular necrotic lesions with distinct dark margins and concentric rings on leaf blades and petioles.
• Progressive chlorosis surrounding lesions leading to premature leaf scorch, defoliation, and canopy thinning.
• Reduced photosynthetic surface area resulting in poor fruit sizing and premature crop maturation.
sunflower_gray_mold.cause: Foliar fungal/bacterial complex. Overwinters on infected crop residues and spreads via wind-driven rain, high humidity (>80%), and temperatures between 20-28°C.
sunflower_gray_mold.organic_treatment:
• Spray Copper Hydroxide (53.8% DF) @ 2.0 g/L or wettable sulfur (2.5 g/L).
• Apply bio-control agent Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis (5 g/L) at 10-day intervals.
• Prune lower infected leaves to promote canopy aeration and reduce humidity.
sunflower_gray_mold.chemical_treatment:
• Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as a protective cover.
• For systemic curative action: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 mL/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 mL/L.
• Re-apply after 12-14 days if wet weather conditions continue.
sunflower_gray_mold.prevention:
• Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-host botanical families.
• Incorporate deep plowing to bury infected crop debris after harvest.
• Maintain balanced soil fertility based on soil test recommendations; avoid high-nitrogen stress.

sunflower_healthy.symptoms:
• Vigorous, uniform green foliage free of visible chlorosis, necrosis, or structural deformation.
• Leaf turgidity, canopy development, and vascular systems appear optimal.
• No active fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect pest colonies observed.
sunflower_healthy.cause: Optimal plant health and robust physiological vitality. No active pathogen infection detected.
sunflower_healthy.organic_treatment:
• Continue maintenance sprays of prophylactic bio-stimulants (seaweed extract, humic acid).
• Apply fermented bio-fertilizers (Jeevarmrut / Panchagavya) at 15-day intervals to strengthen microbial leaf phyllosphere.
• Maintain protective mulch layer to conserve soil moisture and root zone temperature.
sunflower_healthy.chemical_treatment:
• No chemical pesticides or fungicides are required.
• Apply balanced micronutrient spray (Zinc 0.5%, Ferrous 0.5%, Boron 0.2%) during peak vegetative growth if soil tests indicate marginal fertility.
sunflower_healthy.prevention:
• Adhere to balanced N-P-K fertilization schedules; avoid excessive nitrogen that attracts sap-sucking pests.
• Maintain precision irrigation (drip or morning furrow) to prevent extended foliar leaf wetness.
• Conduct weekly crop scouting across field diagonals to catch early isolated pathogen incursions.
